[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#problem-statement]

### Problem Statement

Infrastructure-as-code (Terraform) can be authored to pass human code review while still violating mandatory security or compliance configurations — encryption settings disabled, IAM policies too permissive, required resource tags absent — because reviewers are inconsistent and cannot verify every property on every plan. Once non-compliant infrastructure is provisioned, remediation is disruptive and expensive.
page_texts.5:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#solution-overview]

### Solution Overview

Policy-as-Code Enforcement evaluates the Terraform plan (or Kubernetes manifest) against a library of machine-executable OPA/Rego policies before any cloud resources are provisioned or containers are deployed. Non-compliant plans fail the pipeline with a structured violation report; compliant plans proceed to execution. Policies are versioned alongside the Golden Path catalog and enforced uniformly across all teams and AI-generated infrastructure.
page_texts.6:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#when-to-use]

### When to Use

- Any pipeline that provisions cloud infrastructure via Terraform or deploys Kubernetes manifests
- Any environment where mandatory security configurations (encryption, IAM, network policy) must be systematically enforced
- Any organization adopting autonomous AI development where AI agents generate infrastructure code
page_texts.7:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#benefits]

### Benefits

- Prevents non-compliant infrastructure from ever being provisioned — not after the fact
- Enforces configurations consistently without relying on human reviewer attention
- Produces a policy evaluation report as automatic compliance evidence, eliminating the need to manually document infrastructure security controls

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#target-audience]

## Target Audience

This pattern is intended for the following technical roles:

- **Platform Engineer** — responsible for building and maintaining the policy library and enforcement gate tooling
- **Infrastructure Architect** — designing and governing infrastructure policy rules and compliance standards
- **Security Engineer** — authoring and reviewing Rego policies for security and compliance controls
- **DevOps Engineer** — integrating the policy gate into CI/CD pipelines and maintaining pipeline configurations
page_texts.10:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#business-context]

### Business Context

Gainwell's regulatory obligations (HIPAA, FedRAMP, SOC 2, Medicaid) require that infrastructure configurations meet defined security baselines. These baselines specify mandatory controls: encryption at rest and in transit, minimum replica counts for availability, network isolation, IAM least-privilege enforcement, and mandatory resource tagging for audit traceability. The [Enterprise Architecture Verification Strategy](../../../../strategy/white-papers/engineering/enterprise-architecture-verification-strategy.md) identifies policy-as-code as Layer 3 of the verification architecture — the pre-deployment gate that blocks non-compliant infrastructure before provisioning.
page_texts.11:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#technical-context]

### Technical Context

Gainwell uses Terraform for cloud infrastructure provisioning and Helm/Kubernetes manifests for container workload deployment. CI/CD pipelines (GitHub Actions or Azure Pipelines) run `terraform plan` to produce a structured plan artifact before `terraform apply`. This plan artifact is the evaluation target for policy-as-code enforcement. Open Policy Agent (OPA) with Conftest is the recommended policy evaluation engine; it accepts the JSON-serialized Terraform plan as input and evaluates it against a policy library written in Rego.
page_texts.12:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#problem-details]

### Problem Details

Human review of Terraform plans catches logic errors and obvious misconfigurations, but it cannot reliably catch every policy violation across every resource in a large plan. A reviewer checking a 200-resource Terraform plan for a new environment will miss individual resource-level settings. AI-generated Terraform code may be structurally sound but deviate from Gainwell-specific security baseline requirements that are not represented in the AI model's training data.
page_texts.13:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#forces-and-constraints]

### Forces and Constraints

- Policies must be versioned: infrastructure validated against an older policy version must be re-evaluated when policies are updated
- Policy evaluation must be fast (< 2 minutes for a standard plan) to avoid pipeline friction
- Policies must distinguish between hard violations (plan fails) and soft warnings (plan proceeds with documented deviation)
- Exception process must exist before enforcement is enabled; teams blocked with no recourse route around the gate
page_texts.15:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#pattern-description]

### Pattern Description

The Policy-as-Code Enforcement pattern intercepts the Terraform plan artifact (or Kubernetes manifest set) at a dedicated pipeline stage before any execution step. The policy evaluator loads the current versioned policy library corresponding to the declared Golden Path, evaluates the plan against all applicable policies, and produces a structured evaluation report. Hard-violation failures halt the pipeline; soft warnings are recorded but do not block. The evaluation report is stored as a compliance evidence artifact in the evidence store.

### Architecture Diagram

│  CI/CD Pipeline                                                          │
│                                                                          │

│                            ──────►│    │                      │         │

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#components]

### Components

| Component | Responsibility | Dependencies |
|---|---|---|
| Plan Serializer | Runs `terraform plan -out=tfplan` then `terraform show -json tfplan` to produce the evaluable JSON artifact | Terraform CLI |
| Policy Library | Versioned repository of Rego policies organized by Golden Path class and compliance scope | Golden Path Catalog (PTN-GOV-AI-001) |
| Policy Evaluator | Runs OPA/Conftest against the plan JSON using the applicable policy bundle | Policy Library, OPA runtime |
| Evaluation Report Writer | Serializes evaluation results to the standard evidence schema and attaches as a pipeline artifact | Compliance Evidence Store (PTN-GOV-AI-004) |
| Violation Router | On hard violation: halts pipeline, creates triage ticket, notifies team | AI Governance Policy (PTN-GOV-AI-002) |
page_texts.18:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#interactions]

### Interactions

1. CI/CD pipeline executes `terraform plan` and serializes plan to JSON
2. Policy Gate stage loads the policy bundle for the repository's declared Golden Path and compliance scope
3. Policy Evaluator runs OPA/Conftest; each Rego rule evaluates one or more resource properties and returns ALLOW/DENY with detail
4. Evaluation Report Writer aggregates all rule results into a structured report and attaches to the pipeline run
5. If no hard violations: gate exits 0, `terraform apply` proceeds
6. If any hard violations: Violation Router halts the pipeline, creates a triage ticket with the full report, and notifies the team
page_texts.19:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#variations]

### Variations

- **Kubernetes manifest evaluation**: The same OPA/Conftest evaluation pattern applies to Kubernetes manifests (Helm chart render output) for admission policy checking before deployment
- **Drift re-evaluation**: Scheduled pipeline re-runs evaluate currently deployed infrastructure state (exported via `terraform show`) against the current policy library, detecting policy violations introduced by infrastructure drift or policy updates
- **Multi-environment scoping**: Different policy bundles for development vs. production environments; development policies may permit shorter retention periods or smaller instance sizes that would be hard violations in production

### Prerequisites

- Golden Path Catalog published with compliance metadata (PTN-GOV-AI-001)

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#phase-1-policy-library-foundation]

#### Phase 1: Policy Library Foundation

1. Create a dedicated `golden-path-policies` repository to host the Rego policy library; organize by Golden Path class and compliance scope
2. Implement the baseline policy set covering universal hard violations:
   - All storage resources must have encryption at rest enabled
   - All compute resources must have minimum replica count ≥ 2 for production scope
   - All IAM roles must not use wildcard (`*`) resource bindings
   - All resources must have the required tag set (team, cost-center, compliance-scope, golden-path-id)
   - No public IP assignments on resources tagged with PHI or FedRAMP scope
3. Implement Golden Path-specific policy extensions for the first published paths (e.g., AKS node pool configuration, External Secrets Operator resource present)
4. Write policy unit tests using OPA's built-in test framework; target 100% rule coverage before deployment
page_texts.24:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#phase-2-pipeline-integration]

#### Phase 2: Pipeline Integration

1. Add `terraform show -json` step after `terraform plan` to produce the evaluable artifact
2. Add Policy Gate stage (after plan, before apply) using Conftest with the policy library bound to the declared Golden Path
3. Configure the gate to read the Golden Path declaration from `service.yaml` and select the corresponding policy bundle
4. Deploy in warn-only mode to the first pilot environments; review all soft warnings for promotion to hard violations
5. Switch to deny mode after 2–4 week pilot with acceptable false positive rate

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#phase-3-drift-detection-and-continuous-evaluation]

#### Phase 3: Drift Detection and Continuous Evaluation

1. Configure scheduled pipeline runs (daily) that export current infrastructure state as JSON and re-evaluate against current policy library
2. Integrate policy evaluation results into the compliance dashboard
3. Add policy re-evaluation on policy library version updates — existing deployed infrastructure must be re-checked when policies are updated

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#policy-violation-classification-decision-guide]

### Policy Violation Classification Decision Guide

When authoring a new Rego policy rule, classify it as hard (deny) or soft (warn) using this guide:

| Scenario | Classification | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Compliance control required by HIPAA, FedRAMP, or SOC 2 (e.g., encryption at rest, TLS) | **Hard (deny)** | Regulatory obligation — no discretion |
| Security baseline control (e.g., no public S3 bucket, no root IAM credentials) | **Hard (deny)** | Security posture — violations must not reach production |
| New policy enforcing a practice not previously required | **Soft (warn) → Hard (deny) in 60 days** | Grace period allows teams to remediate without emergency pipeline break |
| Best practice recommendation with no regulatory or security basis | **Soft (warn) only** | Advisory — teams should improve but blocking is disproportionate |
| Policy covering a new resource type not yet widely adopted | **Soft (warn) for 30 days** | Allow teams to report false positives before hardening |
| Performance or cost-efficiency recommendation (e.g., resource limits, tagging) | **Soft (warn) → Hard (deny) with 90-day notice** | Operational concern requiring coordinated rollout |

**Hard vs. soft summary rule:** A policy should be **hard (deny)** if a violation in production would create a compliance obligation, a security incident report, or an on-call page. Everything else is a candidate for soft warning with a hardening timeline.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#example-1-rego-policy--encryption-at-rest]

#### Example 1: Rego Policy — Encryption at Rest

```rego
# policy/common/encryption.rego
package gainwell.common.encryption

import future.keywords.if

deny[msg] if {
    resource := input.resource_changes[_]
    resource.type == "azurerm_storage_account"
    resource.change.after.enable_https_traffic_only == false
    msg := sprintf(
        "HARD VIOLATION [ENC-001]: Storage account '%s' must enforce HTTPS-only traffic. enable_https_traffic_only must be true.",
        [resource.address]
    )
}

deny[msg] if {
    resource := input.resource_changes[_]
    resource.type == "azurerm_storage_account"
    not resource.change.after.blob_properties[_].delete_retention_policy
    msg := sprintf(
        "HARD VIOLATION [ENC-002]: Storage account '%s' must have blob soft delete retention configured.",
        [resource.address]
    )
}
```
page_texts.29:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#example-2-github-actions-policy-gate-step]

#### Example 2: GitHub Actions Policy Gate Step

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- name: Serialize Terraform Plan
  run: terraform show -json tfplan > tfplan.json

- name: Policy-as-Code Enforcement Gate
  uses: gainwell/actions/policy-gate@v1
  with:
    plan_file: tfplan.json
    golden_path: ${{ steps.catalog.outputs.golden_path }}
    policy_library_version: ${{ vars.POLICY_LIBRARY_VERSION }}
    mode: deny  # deny | warn
    evidence_store_url: ${{ vars.EVIDENCE_STORE_URL }}
  env:
    POLICY_LIBRARY_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.POLICY_LIBRARY_TOKEN }}
```
page_texts.31:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#best-practices-this-ensures-new-resource-types-are-allowed-until-explicitly-restricted-reducing-false-positives-during-initial-rollout]

### Best Practices; this ensures new resource types are allowed until explicitly restricted, reducing false positives during initial rollout

- Unit-test every Rego rule before deployment; OPA's native test framework runs in < 1 second for most policy suites
- Separate universal policies (apply to all Golden Paths) from path-specific policies (apply only to a declared path class) — this keeps the policy library maintainable
- Use semantic versioning for the policy library; major version bumps indicate breaking policy changes that require re-evaluation of existing infrastructure
- Treat policy violation rates as a catalog signal: high violation rates for a specific rule may mean the Golden Path template is generating non-compliant defaults, not that teams are deliberately deviating
page_texts.32:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#common-pitfalls]

### Common Pitfalls

- **Evaluating plans too late**: Policy evaluation must occur after `terraform plan` and before `terraform apply`. Evaluating after apply defeats the pre-provisioning gate entirely.
- **Policies without test coverage**: Untested Rego rules have subtle logic errors that produce false positives or missed violations. Always test before deployment.
- **Blanket deny-all then carve out exceptions**: This approach ensures every new resource type is blocked until explicitly permitted, which creates excessive friction. Use targeted deny rules on specific violations instead.
- **Not versioning the policy library**: Teams cannot correlate their infrastructure state to the policy version in effect when it was provisioned. Version the library and record the version in every evaluation report.
- **No soft-warning-to-hard-violation migration path**: Warnings that never graduate to denies are ignored. Define a clear schedule: every soft warning that represents a genuine compliance requirement must graduate to a hard violation within 2 release cycles.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#compliance-requirements]

### Compliance Requirements

- HIPAA § 164.312(a)(2)(iv): Encryption mechanism requirement — enforced via encryption-at-rest and in-transit policies
- FedRAMP AC-6 (Least Privilege): IAM wildcard prohibition policies directly implement this control
- SOC 2 CC6.1: Logical and physical access - IAM and network isolation policies support this criterion
- Policy evaluation reports must be retained for 3 years minimum as compliance evidence
page_texts.36:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#approval-process]

### Approval Process

The policy library requires ARB approval for initial deployment and for every major version bump. Individual rule additions (non-breaking) require peer review by the Platform Engineering team and sign-off by one architect. Policy changes that affect existing approved infrastructure configurations are treated as breaking changes and require ARB review.

| Policy pass rate (all pipelines) | ≥ 98% within 6 months | Evaluation report aggregation |

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#real-world-example-1]

### Real-World Example 1

**Context:** The care-management team's AI agent generates Terraform for a new HIPAA-scoped service. The AI model produces a storage account resource without the `enable_https_traffic_only` flag explicitly set to `true` (it defaults to `false` in older provider versions).

**Implementation:** The policy gate evaluates the Terraform plan and catches the `ENC-001` violation before any resources are provisioned. The pipeline halts. The AI agent context pipeline receives the policy violation report, adds an explicit `enable_https_traffic_only = true` directive to the storage account module, and regenerates. The re-run passes.

**Outcome:** A HIPAA encryption control violation is caught and remediated in minutes with no human review required. No non-compliant infrastructure was ever provisioned.
page_texts.40:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#real-world-example-2]

### Real-World Example 2

**Context:** A compliance audit requires evidence that all HIPAA-scoped infrastructure deployed in Q1 2026 had encryption at rest enabled at provisioning time.

**Implementation:** The auditor queries the compliance evidence store for all policy evaluation reports for HIPAA-scoped repositories in Q1 2026. Each report contains the Terraform plan hash, the policy library version, and the pass/fail result for every encryption rule.

**Outcome:** Audit evidence is produced from a structured query. No manual collection. The evidence is machine-generated at provisioning time and has an unbroken chain of custody.
page_texts.41:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#real-world-example-3]

### Real-World Example 3

**Context:** A new Kubernetes-native workload type is being introduced: CronJobs running PHI batch processing. Several teams start deploying CronJobs with no resource limits (CPU/memory unbounded), which creates a HIPAA availability risk (one misbehaving job can starve the cluster). No existing Rego policy covers CronJobs specifically.

**Implementation:** Platform Engineering authors a new Rego policy: `gainwell.k8s.resource_limits` that applies to Kubernetes CronJob manifests. The policy is unit-tested against 8 synthetic manifests (4 passing, 4 failing covering different violation patterns). The policy enters the library as a soft warning at `version 2026-04.1` with note "will harden to deny in 2026-07-01". All 6 teams with active CronJob deployments receive warning-mode pipeline reports on their next run. 5 teams remediate within 2 weeks. 1 team files an exception citing a fixed-resource third-party job scheduler — the exception is approved with a compensating control (dedicated namespace with ResourceQuota).

**Outcome:** All CronJob workloads are resource-constrained before the hard violation takes effect. The exception process surfaces a gap in the ResourceQuota pattern that is added to the infrastructure catalog in the next quarterly review.

[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#scenario-1-new-cloud-service-integration]

#### Scenario 1: New Cloud Service Integration

A new Azure service type is added to the platform. Before any team can provision it, the Platform Engineering team authors Rego rules for the service type covering mandatory security configurations specific to that service. The rules are reviewed, unit-tested, and deployed to the policy library. Teams subsequently provisioning the new service type are automatically governed from day one.
page_texts.44:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#scenario-2-policy-library-version-migration]

#### Scenario 2: Policy Library Version Migration

A new policy library version introduces a hard violation for missing `cost-center` resource tags (previously a soft warning). All pipelines are updated to reference the new library version. On the next pipeline run for each repository, resources missing the tag produce a hard violation, triggering remediation before any infrastructure is changed.
page_texts.45:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#scenario-3-warning-to-deny-promotion-lifecycle]

#### Scenario 3: Warning-to-Deny Promotion Lifecycle

A new soft warning policy `WARN-NET-002` requires explicit `egress: []` (deny-all egress) in Kubernetes NetworkPolicy resources. The policy enters the library as a warning at `2026-01-01` with a documented " hard violation in 2026-04-01" notice. An automated Jira task is created at warning release, assigned to each adopter team. Over 2 months, 14 of 16 affected teams add explicit egress rules. On `2026-04-01`, the policy is promoted to `deny`. The 2 remaining teams' pipelines fail; both have active exception requests (one is awaiting final approval, one has a 30-day extension granted while migrating to a service mesh). The policy promotion goes live on schedule with no unplanned pipeline breakages.
page_texts.47:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#before-problem-state]

#### Before (Problem State)

- **Non-compliant provisioning**: Terraform plans are reviewed by humans who may miss individual resource property settings; non-compliant infrastructure is provisioned and discovered in compliance audits months later
- **AI-generated infrastructure**: AI-generated Terraform that omits required properties (e.g., `enable_https_traffic_only`) is indistinguishable from human-authored Terraform at plan review time
- **Remediation cost**: Violations discovered post-provisioning require change management, full regression testing, and potential service disruption to remediate
- **Audit evidence**: Demonstrating that all HIPAA-scoped infrastructure had encryption enabled requires humans to manually review Terraform state files or AWS Config data per service
- **Policy drift**: Resource properties that were compliant at provisioning may drift as infrastructure evolves; no systematic re-evaluation mechanism exists
page_texts.48:
[patterns/infrastructure/governance/PTN-INFRA-GOV-002-policy-as-code-enforcement-pattern.md#after-solution-state]

#### After (Solution State)

- **Non-compliant provisioning**: Non-compliant Terraform plans are rejected before provisioning with a specific, actionable violation report referencing the exact resource and property in question
- **AI-generated infrastructure**: AI-generated Terraform is held to the same policy gate as human-authored Terraform; the AI context pipeline regenerates on policy violations without human intervention
- **Remediation cost**: All remediation happens in the development pipeline before any cloud resource is created; the most expensive form of infrastructure remediation (post-deployment change management) is eliminated
- **Audit evidence**: A structured query of the evidence store returns all Q1 2026 HIPAA encryption policy evaluations with Terraform plan hashes in under 5 minutes
- **Policy drift**: Scheduled daily re-evaluations detect configuration drift and alert before drift becomes a compliance finding

## TL;DR

**Problem:** Non-compliant infrastructure configurations (encryption disabled, overly permissive IAM, missing required tags) are provisioned because human review of Terraform plans is inconsistent and cannot catch every property on every resource.

**Solution:** Evaluate the Terraform plan against a versioned OPA/Rego policy library as a hard pre-provisioning gate; block non-compliant plans before any cloud resources are created.

**When to Use:**
- Every pipeline provisioning cloud infrastructure via Terraform
- Every pipeline deploying Kubernetes manifests
- Any team or AI agent generating infrastructure code

**Key Benefits:**
- Prevents non-compliant infrastructure from ever existing in the environment
- Enforces security baselines uniformly without relying on human reviewer attention
- Produces automatic compliance evidence for every provisioning event

**Implementation Complexity:** Medium

**Prerequisites:** Golden Path Catalog (PTN-GOV-AI-001), Verification Contract (PTN-GOV-AI-003), Compliance Evidence Store (PTN-GOV-AI-004), OPA/Conftest in CI/CD runner

**Related Patterns:** PTN-INFRA-GOV-001, PTN-GOV-AI-001, PTN-GOV-AI-003, PTN-GOV-AI-004, PTN-INFRA-API-006
